title: Shortest Path in a Grid
prompt:
A robot starts in the top-left cell of a grid and wants to reach the bottom-right cell. Cells with 0 are open floor, cells with 1 are walls. Each move goes one cell up, down, left or right. Return the fewest moves needed, or -1 if the exit cannot be reached.

Write shortestPath(grid).

shortestPath([
  [0, 0, 0],
  [1, 1, 0],
  [0, 0, 0],
]);  // 4  (right, right, down, down)

shortestPath([
  [0, 1],
  [1, 0],
]);  // -1  (walled in)

Rules: if the start or the exit is a wall, return -1. A 1×1 grid [[0]] needs 0 moves. Grids are at most 100×100.

tests.name: start or exit is a wall
finds the shortest of several routes (not the first one DFS would find)
open 20x20 room needs rows + cols - 2 moves
tests.code:
const grid = Array.from({ length: 20 }, () => Array(20).fill(0));
assertEqual(shortestPath(grid), 38);

hints: Trigger: "fewest moves" / "shortest path" where every move costs the same. That means BFS, not DFS. BFS explores everything 1 move away, then everything 2 moves away, and so on, so the first time it reaches the exit is the shortest.

Idea: put [0, 0, 0] (row, col, distance) in a queue. Repeatedly take the oldest item; if it is the exit, return its distance; otherwise add each open, unvisited neighbour with distance + 1. If the queue empties, return -1.

Code shape: use an array as the queue with a head index (const item = queue[head]; head++) instead of shift(), which is O(n). Add a cell to visited at the moment you push it, so the same cell is never queued twice.
explain:
Time O(rows × cols), space O(rows × cols): every cell enters the queue at most once.

Say it: "All moves cost the same, so BFS gives the shortest path: it visits cells in order of distance, and the first time I reach the exit is the minimum. I mark cells visited when I enqueue them so nothing is processed twice." If moves had different costs (roads with travel times) you would switch to Dijkstra's algorithm, which is BFS with a priority queue instead of a plain queue.
